passages.title: My Friend
passages.text: I have a good friend. He is a student. He likes to eat apples and drink water. He is very happy. We study together every day.

passages.title: My Good Friend Xiao Ming
passages.text: I have a very good friend called Xiao Ming. Xiao Ming is a university student and studies very hard. Every morning he drinks water, eats an apple, and then goes to the library to read. He likes learning new things and also likes helping others. I am very happy to have a friend like him.

passages.title: The Power of Friendship
passages.text: Xiao Ming and I have known each other for five years already. He is my best friend, even though our personalities are very different. He is careful and patient in everything he does, while I am more lively and like taking risks. It is precisely because of these differences that we learn from each other and grow together. When we face difficulties, we always support each other. I think true friendship doesn't require being together every day, but rather being there when the other person needs you.

passages.title: Distance and Longing
passages.text: After graduation, Xiao Ming went to Shanghai for work, while I stayed in Beijing. The distance grew, and opportunities to meet became fewer and fewer, but strangely, the friendship between us didn't fade because of it. Every so often he would send a long message recounting his observations and reflections in his new city; I would also share the small details of daily life with him. Sometimes we would video call and chat until late at night without feeling tired. I gradually came to understand that true friendship is like a deep-rooted tree — it won't wither with the changing of seasons, but only grows thicker with the years. The things we experienced together in our youth have already become part of our shared memories, and no distance can take them away.

passages.title: Friendship and Self-Identity
passages.text: Psychological research shows that the way we choose friends largely reflects our understanding of and expectations for ourselves. The friendships that give us lasting peace of mind tend to be those that have both a high degree of compatibility and sufficient tension — the other person can understand us, yet continuously challenges our fixed ideas from a different perspective. My friendship with Xiao Ming is exactly like this. His steadiness taught me to pause for a moment before acting on impulse, while my emotional nature has at certain moments helped him break through the limits he had set for himself. Sociologists call this kind of relationship a 'developmental friendship': both parties are not just emotional supports, but catalysts for each other's growth. However, the high-speed mobility of modern society makes deep friendship increasingly scarce. People accumulate hundreds of 'contacts' on social media, yet often struggle to find one person who is truly willing to listen. This makes me wonder: in this age of information overload, are we expanding our relationships, or diluting them?

passages.title: On the Nature of Friendship
passages.text: In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle divided friendship into three kinds: friendship based on utility, friendship based on pleasure, and friendship based on virtue. The first two dissolve when the conditions they depend upon disappear; only friendship built on appreciation and respect for each other's character can withstand the test of time. More than two thousand years later, this insight remains profoundly resonant. The atomising tendencies of contemporary society make deep connections between people increasingly difficult. We live amid unprecedented material abundance, yet suffer from a widespread and ineffable loneliness. Sociologist Robert Putnam documented in detail the sustained decline of social capital, and this phenomenon has its corresponding mirror image globally. True friendship requires time, vulnerability, and shared trial — precisely the things that efficiency-driven modern life is least able to provide. Perhaps, while pursuing more connections, what we need even more is to learn how to invest more deeply in fewer relationships.

passages.title: My Cat
passages.text: I have a cat. She is very small and very beautiful. She likes to drink water but does not like to eat books. My dog is also very good. The cat and the dog are good friends.

passages.title: Xiao Hua and Da Huang
passages.text: My home has a cat and a dog. The cat is called Xiao Hua and the dog is called Da Huang. Xiao Hua is very smart and likes to run around the house. Da Huang is very friendly and likes to play in the yard. At first they didn't like each other and often quarrelled. But gradually they became good friends. Now every evening they sleep together — very adorable.

passages.title: Animals Have Feelings Too
passages.text: Anyone who has kept a pet knows that animals, like humans, also have rich emotions. My cat Xiao Hua and dog Da Huang are the best example. Their journey from strangers to familiar companions, from quarrelling to reconciliation, went through a genuine process of emotional development. Scientific research shows that both cats and dogs can feel joy, fear, jealousy, and even sadness. When their owner leaves, they feel lonely; when their owner returns, they show genuine happiness. This makes us think: perhaps the distance between humans and animals is not as far as we imagine.

passages.title: Pets and Modern Loneliness
passages.text: In recent years, the number of pets in Chinese cities has grown sharply. More and more young people are choosing to keep cats or dogs; some attribute this to increasing life pressures, while others see it as reflecting the social trend of rising single-person households. The companionship that pets provide is unconditional — they do not judge, do not demand anything in return, but simply stay quietly by your side. Psychological research has found that interacting with pets can effectively lower cortisol levels and reduce anxiety. However, this kind of relationship also raises some questions worth pondering: as people become increasingly accustomed to forming deep bonds with animals, does this mean that connections between people are becoming more difficult to form? Xiao Hua and Da Huang make me happy, but they cannot replace genuine human friendship. Perhaps pets are a mirror, reflecting what we most desire yet find most difficult to express — to be accepted unconditionally.

passages.title: Emotional Bonds Across Species
passages.text: Cross-disciplinary research at the intersection of ethology and neuroscience is overturning our traditional understanding of animal consciousness. For a long time, Descartes' 'animal-machine' theory provided a philosophical basis for how humans treat other species, holding that animals are nothing more than complex biological machines without genuine capacity for feeling. However, over the past few decades, a large body of empirical research has revealed a strikingly different picture. Primatologists such as Frans de Waal have documented complex empathic behaviours among chimpanzees; neurological research has also confirmed that mammals share brain structures associated with emotional processing. The journey of my cat and dog from opposition to reconciliation may not simply be the result of behavioural conditioning, but an expression of genuine emotional experience. This understanding not only changes how we think about pets, but also poses a profound challenge to the entire system of animal ethics, industrial farming, and anthropocentrism.

passages.title: On the Ethical Reconstruction of the Human-Animal Relationship
passages.titleTranslation: On the Ethical Reconstruction of the Human-Animal Relationship
passages.text: The utilitarian framework proposed by Peter Singer in Animal Liberation, and the rights-based animal ethics system of Tom Regan, represent the most systematic reflection on the human-animal relationship in Western philosophy at the end of the twentieth century. However, both approaches face deep practical difficulties: the former is hard to operationalise due to the complexity of utilitarian calculation; the latter creates fundamental conflicts with many real-world institutions by granting animals inviolable rights. At the same time, traditional Chinese philosophy also contains profound discussions of this issue. The Confucian idea that 'the benevolent person loves people, extending to birds and beasts', and the Taoist realm of 'all things and I are one', both offer dimensions of thought different from the Western discourse of rights. In the face of an increasingly severe ecological crisis, re-examining humanity's place in the community of life is no longer a luxurious speculation confined to philosophers' studies, but an urgent question concerning the survival of our entire species. The cat curled up at my feet for warmth is perhaps the best reminder: our responsibility towards another living being has never needed to wait for philosophy's permission.

passages.text: Today I went to buy apples. The apples were very good and not expensive. I also bought water. I was very happy.

passages.title: Going to the Vegetable Market on the Weekend
passages.titleTranslation: Going to the Vegetable Market on the Weekend
passages.text: Every weekend I like to go to the nearby vegetable market to shop. The vegetables and fruit there are very fresh, and the prices are cheaper than the supermarket too. Today I bought apples, tomatoes, and some green vegetables. The old woman selling apples was very warm and even gave me two extra apples. I spent thirty yuan and bought a lot of things — it felt very good value. On the way home, I was in a great mood.

passages.title: The Disappearing Vegetable Market
passages.text: With the rapid development of urbanisation, traditional open-air vegetable markets are gradually disappearing, being replaced by modern supermarkets and online shopping platforms. Many urban residents have become used to tapping their phone and having vegetables delivered to their door. However, more and more people are beginning to miss the unique atmosphere of life found in the vegetable market. There you can chat with the elderly vendor, select the freshest ingredients, and feel genuine human warmth. The vegetable market is not just a place to buy and sell — it is also a carrier of community culture. In losing it, we lose more than just a way of shopping.

passages.title: The Contest Between the Digital Economy and Traditional Commerce
passages.titleTranslation: The Contest Between the Digital Economy and Traditional Commerce
passages.text: In recent years, fresh produce e-commerce platforms represented by Pinduoduo and Meituan Maicai have risen rapidly, profoundly changing the shopping habits of Chinese urban residents. Data shows that in 2023, the scale of China's fresh produce e-commerce market exceeded 500 billion yuan, with annual growth rates maintained at double digits. This trend has dealt a heavy blow to traditional vegetable markets — foot traffic has decreased, vendors' income has fallen, and some cities have seen large-scale closures. However, the evolution of markets is far from one-directional. More and more cities are beginning to realise that vegetable markets carry not just an economic function, but also serve as a spiritual bond of community life. Some local governments have begun attempting to modernise traditional markets, introducing cold-chain facilities, mobile payment, and online reservation systems, hoping to preserve the human warmth while improving market competitiveness. The tension between tradition and modernity may not necessarily lead to zero-sum confrontation — it may be possible to seek coexistence through innovation.

passages.title: The Market as a Form of Civilisation
passages.titleTranslation: The Market as a Form of Civilisation
passages.text: In his classic study of Moroccan bazaars, anthropologist Clifford Geertz pointed out that markets have never been merely places for the exchange of goods, but are complex spaces for the circulation of information, the reproduction of social relations, and the construction of cultural meaning. Bargaining in the bazaar is not simply economic game-playing, but a ritualised form of social interaction, containing deep codes about trust, identity, and community belonging. China's traditional market culture similarly has this characteristic. From the ancient grass markets and temple fairs to the modern Tianqiao and City God Temple markets, these spaces have always been important carriers of civil society's self-organisation. The current impact of fresh produce e-commerce on traditional markets is, in a certain sense, a process of de-socialisation: transactions are optimised into the most efficient information matching, yet stripped of the interpersonal warmth and cultural depth attached to them. This does not mean that technological progress is necessarily a civilisational regression, but it does require us, when designing new commercial forms, to carefully consider those social values that cannot be quantified by algorithms.

passages.title: The Market, Capital, and the Paradox of the Public
passages.titleTranslation: The Market, Capital, and the Paradox of the Public
passages.text: Within the discourse of economics, the 'market' is a mechanism for resource allocation; in the sociological perspective, it is a refraction of social structure; and at the level of political philosophy, debates surrounding the market are perpetually entangled with the fundamental tension between the public good, state power, and individual freedom. In The Great Transformation, Karl Polanyi profoundly revealed the internal contradictions of market society: once land, labour, and money are commodified, the self-regulating market systematically erodes the very social fabric upon which it depends, thereby generating counter-movements of political protection. The logic of this 'double movement' is being re-enacted in a highly compressed form in the contemporary platform economy. Algorithmic pricing, data monopolies, and the expansion of platform power not only reshape the competitive order in the traditional sense, but profoundly alter the power configuration between public space and private capital. The disappearance of the vegetable market is both a commercial transition at the micro level and a microcosm of the re-adjustment of the triangular relationship between state, capital, and society at the macro level. How to seek a dynamic balance between market efficiency and public values is one of the most pressing shared challenges that this era has left for policy makers and civil society.

passages.title: The First Snow
passages.text: This morning I got up and saw that everything outside was white. It had snowed! This was the year's first snow. I was very happy and immediately put on thick clothes and ran outside. The snow was very soft and the sound of stepping on it was lovely. I made a little snowman out of snow and played snowballs with the neighbour's children. Even though it was very cold, we were all laughing happily. Winter is really wonderful.

passages.title: A Lost Afternoon
passages.text: Last Saturday, I went to a new place by myself. I thought I knew the way, but after walking for a long time I still couldn't find the place I wanted to go. I was a little nervous because my phone had run out of battery and I couldn't use the map. I had no choice but to ask an elderly man on the roadside for directions. He was extremely helpful — not only did he tell me the way, he also accompanied me for a stretch. In the end I found my destination, though an hour late, but feeling very warm inside.

passages.title: The Taste of the Night Market
passages.titleTranslation: The Taste of the Night Market
passages.text: Taiwan's night markets are world-famous. Whenever night falls, the stalls on both sides of the street light up, and the air is filled with the fragrance of all kinds of food. There is grilled squid, stinky tofu, bubble milk tea, and all sorts of snacks I can't name. People jostle shoulder to shoulder, and the sounds of talking and laughter rise and fall. The night market is not just a place to eat — it represents a way of life and cultural identity. For many Taiwanese people, the night market is part of childhood memories, the taste of home. Even after many years away, smelling that familiar fragrance immediately brings back memories of the past.

passages.title: A Letter Never Sent
passages.text: While sorting through old belongings, I found a letter written ten years ago. At that time I had just started university, and missed my hometown and my parents very much. The letter was full of heartfelt words — hopes for the future and anxiety about leaving home. But for some reason, this letter was never sent and was simply buried in an old box. Reading it now feels both strange and familiar. That eighteen-year-old self had so many dreams and so many fears. I think perhaps some words don't need to be spoken — just writing them down is already enough.

passages.title: Grandmother's Kitchen
passages.text: In my memory, grandmother's kitchen was always warm. No matter how the wind blew or the rain fell outside, as soon as you stepped through that small door, you were greeted by the aroma of food and the warmth of the stove. Grandmother couldn't read, but she had a pair of magical hands that could transform the most ordinary ingredients into flavours impossible to forget. She never used a recipe — all the proportions were in the feel of her hands. Every time I asked her how to make something, she would smile and say: 'Just about right will do.' Only later did I understand that within that 'just about right' were hidden decades of experience and a wordless love for her family. Grandmother has been gone for three years, but whenever I smell the fragrance of red-braised pork, that kitchen door slowly opens in my memory.

passages.title: The Last Subway
passages.text: It was late on a Friday night. I had worked overtime until eleven-thirty and just caught the last subway on this line. The carriage was almost empty, with only a scattering of passengers sitting in their respective corners, faces weary. Opposite me sat a middle-aged man in work clothes, his head leaning against the window, already asleep. He was still holding a hard hat in his hands, the corners of his mouth slightly upturned — who knows what he was dreaming of. I suddenly felt that this late-night carriage was like a small shelter, temporarily gathering all the tired people together, running quietly beneath the city. Everyone has somewhere to return to; everyone is working hard for something. This thought gave me an inexplicable sense of warmth.

passages.title: The Limits of Language
passages.text: Wittgenstein once said: 'The limits of my language are the limits of my world.' Learning a new language is not simply a matter of mastering a new set of vocabulary and grammatical rules, but of perceiving and organising reality in an entirely new way. The Japanese word komorebi describes the sight of sunlight falling through the gaps between leaves — a word without a precise equivalent in Chinese or English. The Portuguese word saudade refers to a deep longing and sadness for something absent, and is equally untranslatable. Every language carries the cognitive structures deposited through the long evolution of a particular culture; to learn it is, in a certain sense, to temporarily dwell within another way of being. This also explains why many bilingual people report feeling like different people when thinking in different languages. Language is not merely a tool for expressing thought — it is also the container that shapes thought.

passages.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Boundaries of Human Creativity
passages.titleTranslation: Artificial Intelligence and the Boundaries of Human Creativity
passages.text: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence is reshaping human society's understanding of the concept of 'creativity' to an unprecedented depth. When a language model can generate stylistically accomplished poetry, fiction, and even academic papers within seconds, the meaning of human subjectivity carried by the act of 'creation' comes under fundamental questioning. Critics point out that what artificial intelligence calls 'creation' is nothing more than a statistical summary and rearrangement of existing texts, lacking genuine intentionality and emotional foundation, and can therefore only be the appearance of creativity rather than its essence. Supporters counter, however, that human creativity is similarly built upon the imitation, absorption, and recombination of predecessors' work, and that the two are not fundamentally different at the mechanistic level, differing only in scale and speed. The core of this debate may not lie in whether artificial intelligence 'does or does not' possess creativity, but in why we value human creation in the first place. If the value of a painting lies solely in its visual effect, then machine-generated images are no different from those painted by human hands; but if the value of art lies in the human experience, vulnerability, and search for meaning crystallised in the creative process, then there exists between the two a gulf that cannot simply be bridged. This question is, in essence, a mirror that forces us to examine where precisely the uniqueness of our own existence resides.

passages.title: China's Four Great Inventions
passages.text: Ancient China had four great inventions: papermaking, printing, gunpowder, and the compass. These four inventions changed the history of the world. Papermaking allowed people to write down and preserve knowledge. Printing allowed books to be produced in large quantities, so more people could read. Gunpowder was initially used for celebrations, and later used in warfare. The compass helped people find direction at sea, making ocean voyages possible. These inventions spread from China to all parts of the world and made great contributions to the development of human civilisation.

passages.title: Beijing: A City of the Ancient and the Modern
passages.titleTranslation: Beijing: A City of the Ancient and the Modern
passages.text: Beijing is the capital of China and also an ancient city with more than three thousand years of history. There are many famous historical sites here, such as the Forbidden City, the Great Wall, and the Temple of Heaven. The Forbidden City was the residence of emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties, with more than nine thousand rooms inside. The Great Wall stretches several thousand kilometres from east to west and is China's most famous structure. Besides historical sites, Beijing is also a modern metropolis with many tall buildings, subways, and shopping centres. Beijing's food is also very famous — the most well-known is Peking roast duck. If you come to China, you must go and see Beijing.

passages.title: Confucius: The Thinker Who Changed China
passages.titleTranslation: Confucius: The Thinker Who Changed China
passages.text: Confucius is one of the greatest thinkers and educators in Chinese history. He lived in the Spring and Autumn period two thousand five hundred years ago, and devoted his life to promoting moral concepts such as benevolence, righteousness, and ritual propriety. Confucius believed that a person should continuously study and cultivate their character in order to contribute to society. His educational philosophy was very advanced — he advocated teaching each student according to their particular characteristics. His teachings were later compiled by his followers into the Analects, which became one of the most important classics in China for thousands of years. Confucius's ideas influenced not only China but also had a profound impact on Asian countries such as Japan, Korea, and Vietnam. To this day, Confucian thought remains a key to understanding Chinese culture.

passages.title: Chinese New Year
passages.text: The Spring Festival is the most important traditional holiday in China, also called the Lunar New Year. Every year in January or February, Chinese people celebrate the Spring Festival. Before the festival, people clean their houses, buy new clothes, and prepare lots of delicious food. On New Year's Eve, the whole family eats the reunion dinner together and watches the Spring Festival Gala programme. When the New Year arrives, children receive red envelopes containing lucky money. On the streets there are dragon and lion dances, and many fireworks. The Spring Festival is generally celebrated for fifteen days — the last day is called the Lantern Festival, when people eat glutinous rice balls and watch lantern displays. For Chinese people, the Spring Festival is a time to return home and reunite with family, the warmest time of the year.

passages.title: Tu Youyou: Saving Lives with Artemisinin
passages.titleTranslation: Tu Youyou: Saving Lives with Artemisinin
passages.text: Tu Youyou is a famous Chinese pharmacologist and the first Chinese scientist to receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Born in 1930, she developed a strong interest in medicine from a young age. In the 1960s and 70s, malaria was claiming vast numbers of lives around the world, and the drugs available at the time could no longer effectively control the disease. Tu Youyou led a team that studied ancient Chinese medical texts in depth, searching for clues among hundreds of traditional herbs. After countless failures, she finally extracted the active ingredient from sweet wormwood — artemisinin. This drug has saved millions of lives, particularly among children in Africa. In 2015 she received the Nobel Prize, proving to the world the value of traditional Chinese medical wisdom. Her story tells us that perseverance and patience are the most important qualities in scientific exploration.

passages.title: The Great Wall: Witness to History
passages.titleTranslation: The Great Wall: Witness to History
passages.text: The Great Wall is one of the most monumental construction projects in human history, stretching over twenty thousand kilometres across several provinces in northern China. The construction of the Great Wall began during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, when various feudal states built separate sections of wall to resist the invasions of northern nomadic peoples. After the First Emperor of Qin unified the six states, he connected these scattered sections of wall, forming the earliest version of the Great Wall in the proper sense. Through subsequent repairs and expansions during the Han, Ming, and other dynasties, the Great Wall gradually evolved into the scale we see today. However, the significance of the Great Wall goes far beyond military defence. It is the embodiment of the ancient Chinese state's will; millions of labourers built with their blood and sweat this miracle of human civilisation that is nearly impossible to replicate. Today the Great Wall has become one of China's most important cultural symbols, attracting tens of millions of visitors each year. However, with the passage of time and the impact of human activity, the work of protecting the Wall faces increasingly serious challenges.

passages.title: Li Bai: The Legendary Life of the Poet Immortal
passages.titleTranslation: Li Bai: The Legendary Life of the Poet Immortal
passages.text: Li Bai (701-762) is one of the greatest poets in Chinese literary history, revered by posterity as the 'Poet Immortal'. Born during the height of the Tang dynasty, he spent his life wandering the world, leaving his footprints across more than half of China. Compared to his contemporary Du Fu, Li Bai's poetry is more free-spirited and uninhibited, filled with a love of nature, a yearning for freedom, and a profound sense of life's impermanence. His representative works including Quiet Night Thoughts, Bring in the Wine, and Gazing at Lushan Waterfall have been recited for hundreds of years and become iconic symbols of Chinese culture. Li Bai's official career was filled with setbacks; though he briefly served in the court of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, he was marginalised due to his uninhibited personality and inability to flatter. He chose to return to the mountains and rivers, taking wine as his companion and using poetry to record the wild joy and deep sorrow of his inner world. According to legend, he finally fell drunk into a river, drowned while trying to grasp the reflection of the moon — a legend that is itself the best footnote to his legendary life.

passages.title: Chinese Tea Culture
passages.text: Tea, as one of China's most important cultural symbols, has a history traceable to more than four thousand years ago during the era of the Divine Farmer. Legend has it that when the Divine Farmer was tasting hundreds of plants, he accidentally discovered that tea leaves had detoxifying properties, thereby beginning humanity's long affinity with tea. However, tea truly entered the daily life of ordinary people only after the Tang dynasty. The Classic of Tea written by Lu Yu is the world's first monograph on tea, systematically expounding the way of cultivating, processing, preparing, and appreciating tea, elevating tea-drinking from a purely utilitarian act to a refined cultural art. Tea culture reached its peak during the Song dynasty, when 'tea competitions' emerged as a unique social custom. During the Ming and Qing dynasties, methods of brewing tea gradually shifted from compressed and powdered tea to loose-leaf tea, laying the foundation for the modern Chinese way of drinking tea. To this day, Chinese tea culture encompasses multiple dimensions including tea ceremony, tea art, the tea trade, and the Ancient Tea Horse Road — it is both a part of daily life and an important vehicle through which China exports cultural soft power to the world.

passages.title: Reform and Opening Up and China's Economic Miracle
passages.titleTranslation: Reform and Opening Up and China's Economic Miracle
passages.text: In 1978, the Reform and Opening Up policy promoted by Deng Xiaoping initiated the most profound socioeconomic transformation in Chinese history. In the more than forty years since, China's economic scale grew from less than two percent of global GDP to approximately eighteen percent, becoming the world's second-largest economy, with hundreds of millions of people lifted out of poverty in the process. This achievement has no precedent in human history, and economists have called it the 'China Miracle'. The core logic of Reform and Opening Up was to selectively introduce market mechanisms within the framework of the socialist system, using special economic zones as pilot projects and export-oriented development as a driving force, gradually integrating China into global value chains. Shenzhen's development from a small fishing village into an international metropolis with a population of over ten million is the most representative microcosm of this process. However, this high-speed growth was also accompanied by a series of deep-rooted contradictions, including widening regional imbalances, rising environmental pressures, and an expanding wealth gap. How to achieve more inclusive and sustainable growth while maintaining development momentum is one of the core policy challenges China currently faces.

passages.title: The Origin and Evolution of Chinese Characters
passages.titleTranslation: The Origin and Evolution of Chinese Characters
passages.text: Chinese characters constitute the world's only ancient writing system that has never been interrupted, with a developmental lineage spanning more than three thousand years, bearing the entire memory of the evolution of Chinese civilisation. The earliest mature system of Chinese characters is found in the oracle bone inscriptions of the Shang dynasty — divination texts carved on turtle shells and animal bones dating back approximately 3,300 years. These early characters already displayed the rudimentary forms of the character-formation principles of pictography, ideography, compound ideography, and phono-semantic composition, laying the foundation for the 'Six Scripts' theory applied by later generations. Through the evolution of bronze inscriptions, large seal script, and small seal script, Chinese characters achieved the unification of script under the Qin dynasty, a political measure that had far-reaching implications for the continuity of Chinese civilisation. The logographic nature of Chinese characters creates a fundamental cognitive difference from alphabetic writing: research indicates that reading Chinese relies more on the right brain's holistic pattern recognition, while alphabetic writing relies more on the left brain's linear decoding. Whether this cognitive difference shapes different ways of thinking in its users remains a hot topic at the intersection of linguistics and cognitive science. In the dual context of globalisation and digitalisation, Chinese characters are undergoing yet another profound morphological evolution — emoji, input methods, and cross-linguistic transmission are reshaping the vitality of this ancient symbol system in ways that ancient people could not have anticipated.

passages.text:
I like windsurfing. The windsurfing board is on the water. I stand on the board. The wind is strong. I am very happy.

My friend also likes windsurfing. He goes to the water every day. The water is very blue. The wind is good. We play together.

Windsurfing is a lot of fun. Do you like windsurfing?

passages.title: Learning to Windsurf
passages.text:
I started learning to windsurf. The teacher said windsurfing is not difficult, but you need to practice. I go to the seaside every weekend to practice.

The first time, I stepped on the board and fell into the water right away. The teacher said: 'It's okay, try again.' I slowly learned to stand steady. When the wind comes, I hold the sail with my hands. The sail is very big and the wind is strong.

Now I can move on the water for a while. I am very happy. Next month, I want to join a competition. My friend says I am improving quickly. I think about windsurfing every day.

passages.title: A Windsurfing Competition
passages.text:
Last Saturday, I took part in a windsurfing competition. The competition was held at the seaside, and many people participated. I was a little nervous, but also very excited.

The competition started. The wind blew from the north and was very fast. I worked hard to control the sail and let the board follow the wind. The waves were not too high, which was easier for me. I slowly overtook several competitors and felt great.

Near the end of the race, a sudden strong gust of wind came. I almost fell into the water, but I held on. In the end, I came in third place. The coach said my technique had improved a lot and told me to keep working hard. I plan to enter another competition next month — this time I want to come in first.

passages.title: Little Red Riding Hood
passages.text:
A girl lives in a small village. Her name is Little Red Riding Hood. She wears a red hood every day. She loves her grandmother very much. Her grandmother lives in the forest.

One morning, her mother makes a cake. "Take this cake to Grandmother," she says. "Stay on the path. Do not talk to strangers." Little Red Riding Hood takes the cake. She walks into the forest.

In the forest, she meets a wolf. The wolf is big. The wolf is bad. "Hello, little girl," he says. "Where do you go?" "I go to my grandmother's house," she says. The wolf smiles. He has a plan.

The wolf runs to Grandmother's house. He knocks on the door. "Who is it?" asks Grandmother. "It's me!" says the wolf. He opens the door. He eats Grandmother! Then he wears her clothes. He lies down in her bed.

Little Red Riding Hood arrives at the house. She sees Grandmother in the bed. "Grandmother, why do you have such big eyes?" she asks. "To see you better," says the wolf. "Grandmother, why do you have such big ears?" she asks. "To hear you better," says the wolf. "Grandmother, why do you have such big teeth?" she asks. "To eat you better!" says the wolf.

The wolf jumps out of the bed. A hunter hears the noise. He runs into the house. He saves Little Red Riding Hood. He saves Grandmother too. The wolf runs away. Little Red Riding Hood is happy. She never talks to strangers again.

passages.title: The Bremen Town Musicians
passages.text:
A donkey lives on a farm. He is old. He cannot work anymore. His owner wants to get rid of him. The donkey is sad. He runs away. He wants to go to Bremen. He wants to be a musician there.

On the road, he meets a dog. The dog is old too. He cannot hunt anymore. His owner wants to get rid of him. "Come with me to Bremen," says the donkey. "We can make music together." The dog is happy. They walk together.

They meet a cat. The cat is old. She cannot catch mice anymore. Her owner wants to get rid of her. "Come with us to Bremen," says the donkey. The cat is happy. Now three animals walk together.

They meet a rooster. The rooster is scared. "My owner wants to cook me!" he says. "Come with us to Bremen," says the donkey. The rooster is happy. Now four animals walk together.

Night comes. The animals see a small house. There is light inside. They look through the window. Robbers sit at a table. The table has lots of food. The animals are hungry. They make a plan.

The donkey stands at the window. The dog stands on the donkey. The cat stands on the dog. The rooster stands on the cat. They make a big noise together. The robbers are scared. They run away. The animals eat the food. They live happily in the house.

passages.title: Hansel and Gretel
passages.text:
A boy and a girl live near a forest. The boy is Hansel. The girl is Gretel. Their family is poor. They do not have much food. Their mother wants to leave them in the forest.

Hansel hears the plan. At night, he collects white stones. The next day, the parents take the children into the forest. Hansel drops the stones on the path. The parents leave the children alone.

Night comes. The children follow the stones home. Their mother is angry. She wants to leave them in the forest again. This time, Hansel cannot collect stones. The door is locked. He uses bread instead.

The parents take them into the forest again. Hansel drops small pieces of bread. But birds eat the bread. The children cannot find the way home. They are lost in the forest.

They find a house. The house is made of candy! They are hungry. They eat the walls. An old woman opens the door. "Come inside, children," she says. But the woman is a witch. She wants to eat them.

The witch locks Hansel in a cage. She makes Gretel work. One day, the witch wants to cook Hansel. She tells Gretel to check the oven. Gretel pushes the witch into the oven instead. She frees Hansel. They find gold in the house. They take the gold. They go home. They live happily with their father.

The witch locks Hansel in a cage. She makes Gretel work. One day, the witch wants to cook Hansel. She tells Gretel to check the oven. Gretel pushes the witch into the oven instead. The children run away. They find gold in the house. They go home. They live happily with their father.

passages.title: Snow White
passages.text:
A long time ago, a queen wished for a child. She wanted a daughter with skin as white as snow. Soon, she had a baby girl. She named her Snow White. But the queen died. The king married a new queen. The new queen was very vain. She had a magic mirror.

Every day, the queen asked the mirror a question. "Mirror, mirror, on the wall, who is the prettiest of them all?" For years, the mirror said the queen. But one day, the mirror said Snow White. The queen became very angry. She called a huntsman. "Take Snow White into the forest," she said. "Kill her there." But the huntsman felt sorry for Snow White. He let her go.

Snow White walked through the forest. She found a small house. Seven dwarfs lived there. They said she could stay. Every day, the dwarfs went to work. Snow White cooked and cleaned for them. She was happy in the little house.

The queen asked her mirror again. "Mirror, mirror, on the wall, who is the prettiest of them all?" The mirror said Snow White was still alive. The queen was furious. She dressed as an old woman. She made a poisoned apple. She walked to the dwarfs' house. She gave the apple to Snow White. Snow White took a bite. She fell to the ground.

The dwarfs came home. They found Snow White on the floor. They thought she was dead. They cried for many days. They put her in a glass coffin. One day, a prince rode by. He saw Snow White in the coffin. He fell in love with her.

The prince's servants carried the coffin. One servant stumbled. The piece of apple fell out of Snow White's mouth. She woke up! The prince asked her to marry him. Snow White said yes. They lived happily together. The evil queen never bothered her again.

passages.title: Cinderella
passages.text:
Cinderella lived with her stepmother and two stepsisters. Her mother had died many years ago. Cinderella planted a small tree by her mother's grave. She cried under the tree every day. The tree grew tall. Her stepmother did not like her. Her stepsisters were unkind too. They made Cinderella do all the housework.

One day, an invitation arrived. The king invited every young woman to a royal ball. The stepsisters got ready for the ball. Cinderella wanted to go too. But she had nothing nice to wear. Her stepsisters laughed at her. They left for the ball without her.

Cinderella cried by her mother's grave. "Little tree, shake and shiver," she said. "Give me something silver and golden." Suddenly, two white birds flew down. They brought a beautiful dress. They also brought gold slippers. Cinderella put on the dress and slippers.

Cinderella arrived at the ball. The prince saw her immediately. He asked her to dance. They danced all night together. Cinderella forgot the time. Suddenly, she remembered she must leave. She ran down the stairs. She lost one gold slipper on the steps.

The next day, the prince searched the kingdom. He carried the gold slipper with him. Every young woman tried on the slipper. But it did not fit anyone. Finally, the prince came to Cinderella's house. Both stepsisters tried the slipper. It did not fit them.

Then Cinderella tried the slipper. It fit her perfectly! The prince recognized her from the ball. He asked her to marry him. Cinderella said yes. They got married in the palace. They lived happily ever after.

passages.title: Rumpelstiltskin
passages.text:
A poor miller had a beautiful daughter. One day, he met the king. He boasted, "My daughter can spin straw into gold." The king was interested. He brought the girl to the palace. He locked her in a room full of straw. "Spin this into gold by morning," he said. "Or you will die."

The girl sat alone and cried. Suddenly, a strange little man appeared. "Why are you crying?" he asked. "I must spin this straw into gold," she said. "What will you give me if I spin it for you?" he asked. She gave him her necklace. The little man spun all the straw into gold.

The next morning, the king was delighted. He locked the girl in an even bigger room. Again, the little man appeared. This time, she gave him her ring. He spun all the straw into gold again. The king was very pleased.

On the third night, the king locked her in the biggest room. "If you succeed again," he said, "I will marry you." The little man appeared once more. "What will you give me if I spin it for you?" he asked. This time, she had nothing to give him. "Promise me your first child," he said. She was desperate, so she agreed. He spun the straw into gold.

The king married the girl. She became queen. A year later, she had a baby. Then the little man returned. "Give me the child," he said. The queen begged him to let her keep the baby. He felt sorry for her. "You have three days to guess my name," he said.

The queen sent a messenger into the forest. By chance, he heard the little man singing a strange song. He sang, "Oh, how good that no one knows, that my name is Rumpelstiltskin!" The messenger ran back and told the queen. When the little man returned, the queen said his name. He was furious. He stamped his foot and disappeared forever. The queen kept her child.

passages.title: Bluebeard
passages.text:
A rich man lives in a castle. He has a blue beard. People call him Bluebeard. He wants a wife. Many women feel scared of him. But one young woman agrees. They marry that same week.

One day, Bluebeard must travel. "Here are all my keys," he says. "You may open every room. But do not open this one small door. This key opens the small room." He points to a tiny gold key. "Never use this key," he warns. Then he leaves the castle.

The young woman explores the castle. She opens many beautiful rooms. She sees gold and silver everywhere. But she thinks about the small door. She feels very curious. Finally, she cannot wait anymore. She walks to the small door. She puts the key in the lock.

She opens the door slowly. The room is dark and quiet. She sees hints of something terrible. Other wives were here before. Something bad happened to them. The young woman feels very afraid. She drops the key in shock. The key falls to the floor. She picks the key up quickly. She runs from the room. She locks the door again.

She tries to clean the key. She wipes it again and again. But a strange mark stays on it. It will not go away. The young woman feels very worried. Bluebeard will know her secret.

Bluebeard returns home that night. "Give me all the keys," he says. He counts the keys carefully. He sees the mark on one key. "You opened the small room!" he shouts. He becomes very angry. The young woman begs for time. "Let me pray first," she says. She runs upstairs to a tower. She calls for her sister. "Look for our brothers," she cries. "Tell them to come quickly!"

Bluebeard climbs the stairs, angry. He wants to punish her now. Suddenly, the door bursts open. Her two brothers run inside. They stop Bluebeard right there. They protect their sister bravely. The young woman is safe at last. She inherits Bluebeard's whole castle. She lives happily ever after.

passages.title: Puss in Boots
passages.text:
A poor miller dies. He has three sons. The oldest son gets the mill. The second son gets a donkey. The youngest son gets only a cat. "What can I do with a cat?" he asks. He feels very sad.

But the cat can talk! "Don't worry," says the cat. "Give me a bag. Give me a pair of boots. I will help you." The young man is surprised. He gives the cat boots. He gives the cat a bag. The cat puts on the boots. He looks very proud.

The cat catches a rabbit. He puts it in his bag. He walks to the king's castle. "This rabbit is a gift," says the cat. "It is from my master, the Marquis of Carabas." The king is pleased. The cat brings more gifts every week. The king likes the Marquis very much.

One day, the cat has a plan. "Go swim in the river," he tells his master. The young man swims. The cat hides his master's clothes. Then the king's carriage passes by. "Help!" "Thieves stole my master's clothes!" shouts the cat. The king gives the young man new clothes. The young man looks like a real marquis now. The king invites him into the carriage.

The cat runs ahead. He finds a huge castle. A scary ogre lives there. The ogre can change into animals. "Can you become a lion?" asks the cat. The ogre becomes a lion. The cat is scared but clever. "But can you become small?" asks the cat. "Can you become a mouse?" The ogre becomes a mouse. The cat jumps on the mouse. He eats the ogre at once!

The king's carriage arrives at the castle. "This is my master's castle," says the cat. The king is very impressed. He meets the young man again. The king's daughter falls in love with him. They marry that same day. The young man becomes a real marquis. The clever cat lives in the castle too. He never has to catch mice again.

passages.title: Tom Thumb
passages.text:
A poor woodcutter has seven sons. The youngest son is very small. They call him Tom Thumb. The family has no food. The parents feel very worried. One night, they make a hard choice. They decide to leave the children. They will lose them in the forest.

Tom Thumb hears the parents' plan. He is small but smart. He goes outside that night. He fills his pockets with stones. The next day, they walk far. The parents leave the children alone. The other brothers cry loudly. But Tom Thumb has a plan. He drops white stones along the path. The stones shine in the moonlight. That night, the brothers follow the stones. They find their way home!

The parents are happy to see them. But soon, they have no food again. They decide to leave the children again. This time, Tom Thumb has no stones. He drops bread crumbs instead. But birds eat all the crumbs! Now the children are truly lost. They walk through the dark forest.

The children see a light. They find a big house. An ogre lives in this house. His wife lets them come inside. She gives them food and a warm bed. But the ogre comes home. "I smell children!" he shouts. His wife hides the children. But the ogre finds them anyway.

The ogre has seven daughters too. They sleep in the same room. Tom Thumb has a clever idea. At night, he swaps the hats. The children wear the ogre's daughters' crowns. The daughters wear the children's hats. In the dark, the ogre makes a mistake. He hurts his own daughters instead! The children escape quickly.

The ogre wakes up and chases them. He wears magic seven-league boots. Each step covers many miles. He gets tired and falls asleep. Tom Thumb sneaks up carefully. He steals the ogre's magic boots! Now Tom Thumb can travel fast too. He puts on the huge boots. He runs home in a single day. He brings his family gold from the ogre's house. The family never feels hungry again.

passages.title: Bluebeard
passages.text:
A wealthy man lived in a large castle in a distant province. His beard was an unusual shade of blue, so people called him Bluebeard. He wanted to marry, but many women were afraid of his strange appearance. Eventually, a young woman who lived nearby agreed to marry him, and they got married that same week.

Soon after the wedding, Bluebeard had to leave on a journey. Before he left, he gave his wife a large ring of keys. "These keys open every room in the castle," he said. "You may explore any room you like while I am away. But you must never open this one small door. This key opens the small room, and you must never use it." He pointed to a tiny golden key and warned her one more time before he left the castle.

The young woman explored the castle with great excitement, and she opened many beautiful rooms full of gold and silver. Still, she kept thinking about the small forbidden door, and her curiosity grew stronger with every passing hour. Finally, she could not wait any longer, so she walked to the small door and put the key in the lock.

She opened the door slowly and looked inside, but the room was dark and completely silent. She saw signs of something terrible on the floor, and she realized other wives had been here before her. Something bad had clearly happened to them, and the young woman felt a deep, sudden fear. In her shock, she dropped the key, and it fell to the floor. She picked it up quickly, ran from the room, and locked the door again with shaking hands.

She tried to clean the key, but a strange mark remained on it. No matter how hard she rubbed, the mark would not disappear. The young woman felt more and more worried, because she knew that Bluebeard would soon discover her secret.

That night, Bluebeard returned home earlier than expected, and he demanded, "Give me all the keys." He counted them carefully, one by one, and when he reached the small golden key, he saw the mark right away. "You opened the small room!" he shouted angrily, and he became extremely angry as he moved toward her. The young woman begged him for a little more time, saying, "Let me pray first." She ran up the stairs to a high tower and called out to her sister for help. "Look for our brothers," she cried out, "and tell them to come here quickly!"

Bluebeard climbed the stairs after her, still full of anger, because he wanted to punish her right away. Suddenly, the door burst open with great force, and her two brothers ran into the room immediately. They stopped Bluebeard before he could hurt her, and they protected their sister bravely and without fear. The young woman was finally safe, and she inherited Bluebeard's entire castle and all his wealth. From that day on, she lived a happy and peaceful life.

passages.title: Puss in Boots
passages.text:
An old miller died and left very little behind for his three sons. The oldest son received the mill, and the second son received a donkey. The youngest son received only an ordinary cat, and he wondered sadly, "What good can come from owning a cat?" He felt he had received the worst share of all.

To his great surprise, the cat suddenly began to speak, and it said with confidence, "Don't worry." "Just give me a strong sack and a good pair of boots, and I will help you." The young man agreed, though he doubted it would work, and he gave the cat both items. The cat put on the boots and looked extremely proud of himself.

The cat caught a rabbit, placed it inside his sack, and walked straight to the king's castle. "This rabbit is a gift from my master, the Marquis of Carabas," he explained. The king was very pleased with such a thoughtful gift. Every week after that, the cat brought more gifts, and over time, the king grew genuinely fond of the mysterious marquis.

One day, the clever cat came up with an ambitious plan. He told his master to go swimming in the river nearby. While the young man swam, the cat hid his master's old clothes. Soon after, the king's royal carriage happened to pass by that very spot. "Help! Thieves have stolen my master's clothes!" the cat shouted loudly. Moved by pity, the king gave the young man fine new clothing. Now dressed elegantly, the young man truly looked like a real marquis. The king then invited him to ride along in the royal carriage.

The cat ran ahead of the carriage toward a distant, enormous castle. A frightening ogre lived there, and he had the magical power to transform into absolutely any creature. "Can you turn yourself into a lion?" the cat asked boldly. The ogre immediately transformed into a huge, terrifying lion, but the clever cat, though frightened, quickly thought of another idea. "But surely you cannot turn into something as small as a mouse," the cat said slyly. Unable to resist the challenge, the ogre transformed himself into a small mouse. The cat pounced on the mouse instantly and ate him at once.

The royal carriage finally arrived at the castle, and the cat proudly announced, "This is my master's castle." The king was thoroughly impressed, and he greeted the young man warmly once again. The king's daughter fell deeply in love with him, and the couple married that very same day. The young man became a true marquis, and the clever cat continued living comfortably in the castle. He never again needed to hunt for his own mice.

passages.title: Momotaro
passages.text:
Long ago, an old man and woman lived near a river. They had no children, and they felt very lonely. One day, the old woman washed clothes by the river. Suddenly, a giant peach floated toward her. Momotaro grew up quickly and became very strong. His parents loved him more than anything in the world. One day, he heard about fierce demons on a distant island. These demons often attacked villages and stole valuable treasure. Momotaro decided to fight the demons and protect his people. His mother made him delicious millet dumplings for the journey. He said goodbye to his parents and left the house.

On his way, Momotaro met a hungry dog on the road. "Will you give me a dumpling?" asked the dog politely. Momotaro shared one dumpling, and the dog joined his journey. Soon after, he met a monkey sitting in a tree. The monkey also wanted a dumpling and offered to help. Momotaro agreed, and the monkey climbed down happily. Finally, a pheasant flew down and asked for food. Momotaro gave the bird a dumpling, and it joined the group too.

Fierce demons guarded the gates with long, sharp spears. The pheasant flew high and attacked the demons from above. The monkey climbed the walls and scratched the demons hard. The dog bit the demons' legs and made them fall. Momotaro fought bravely with his sword and defeated their leader.

The demon leader begged Momotaro for mercy and forgiveness. He promised to stop attacking villages and return all the treasure. Momotaro accepted his promise and stopped the fight. The demons brought out gold, jewels, and other stolen treasure. Momotaro and his friends loaded everything onto their boat. They sailed home across the sea with great joy. His parents welcomed him with tears and warm hugs. From that day, the village lived in peace and happiness.

passages.title: Urashima Taro
passages.text:
A young fisherman named Urashima Taro lived in a small village. He was kind to all animals and often helped them. One day, he saw children hurting a small turtle on the beach. Urashima Taro stopped the children and saved the turtle's life. He gently placed the turtle back into the sea. The turtle thanked him and swam away quickly.

A few days later, the same turtle returned to the shore. "Thank you for saving me," said the turtle with a smile. "Please climb onto my back, and I will thank you properly." Urashima Taro climbed onto the turtle's back with curiosity. The turtle swam deep beneath the waves toward the ocean floor. Soon, they arrived at a magnificent underwater palace.

A beautiful princess named Otohime welcomed him at the palace. "Thank you for saving my turtle," she said warmly. She invited Urashima Taro to stay and enjoy her kingdom. He ate delicious food and watched colorful fish dance. Time passed pleasantly, and he forgot about his old life. But after three days, he began to miss his village. He told the princess that he needed to go home.

The princess gave him a beautiful box as a farewell gift. "Never open this box, no matter what happens," she warned him. Urashima Taro promised to keep her box closed forever. The turtle carried him back to his own village happily. But when he arrived, everything looked strange and different. He could not find his house or any familiar faces. An old man told him the village's history from long ago.

Urashima Taro learned that three hundred years had actually passed. Confused and sad, he opened the princess's forbidden box. White smoke poured out and surrounded him completely. Instantly, Urashima Taro's hair turned white, and his body grew old. The three days in the palace had been three hundred years on land. He realized the box had held his true, missing age. Urashima Taro lived the rest of his life peacefully by the sea.

passages.title: The Grateful Crane
passages.text:
An old man found an injured crane trapped in a hunter's net. He carefully freed the crane and helped it fly away. That night, a beautiful young woman knocked on his door. She said that she was cold, lost, and had nowhere to go. The old man and his wife welcomed her into their home. The young woman decided to stay and help the poor couple.

The young woman offered to weave beautiful cloth for the family. "Please do not watch me while I am weaving," she requested. The couple agreed and waited patiently outside the room. Days later, she gave them a stunning piece of silk cloth. The old man sold the cloth for a very high price. The family used the money to buy food and clothes.

The young woman wove more beautiful cloth many times after that. Each time, she asked the couple not to watch her work. The family became wealthier and happier with every piece of cloth. But the old man grew very curious about her secret. One day, he could not control his curiosity any longer. Quietly, he opened the door and looked inside the room.

Inside, he saw a crane pulling feathers from its own body. The crane was weaving the beautiful cloth with its feathers. Shocked, the old man realized the young woman was actually the crane. The crane noticed him watching and stopped weaving immediately. She turned to him with sad, gentle eyes. "You have seen my true form now," she said quietly.

"I am the crane you saved from the hunter's net. I came to repay your kindness with my weaving." The crane explained that she could not stay any longer. She thanked the old man and his wife for their kindness. Slowly, she transformed back into a beautiful white crane. The crane flew out the window and into the sky. The old man never saw her again, but he never forgot her kindness.

passages.title: Momotaro
passages.text:
Long ago, in a quiet village beside a river, an elderly couple lived out their days with a quiet ache: despite decades of marriage, they had never been blessed with a child of their own. One morning, as the old woman knelt by the riverbank washing clothes, she noticed an enormous peach bobbing toward her on the current, far larger than any she had ever seen. Delighted by such an unusual find, she carried it home with great excitement, eager to share it with her husband. When he split the peach open that evening, they were astonished to discover a baby boy nestled inside, as though the fruit itself had been waiting to deliver him into their care. Overjoyed, they named him Momotaro — literally "peach boy" — and resolved to raise him as their own.

Under their devoted care, Momotaro grew with startling speed, and it was not long before he possessed both extraordinary strength and a fierce sense of justice. His parents doted on him endlessly, though they also sensed, with a mixture of pride and apprehension, that he was destined for something greater than village life. Word eventually reached him of a band of demons terrorizing a distant island, plundering villages and hoarding whatever treasure they could seize. Rather than shrink from the danger, Momotaro announced his intention to confront the demons himself and put an end to their reign of terror. His mother, though heartbroken at the thought of his departure, prepared a batch of millet dumplings to sustain him on his journey, and with a solemn farewell, he set out toward the coast.

He had not traveled far before he encountered a half-starved dog lingering by the roadside. "Would you spare one of your dumplings?" the dog asked, with more courtesy than one might expect from a stray. Moved by its plight, Momotaro shared his food freely, and the grateful dog fell into step beside him. Not long afterward, a monkey perched in a nearby tree made a similar request, and having proven himself equally generous, Momotaro soon found the monkey scrambling down to join his growing company. Finally, a pheasant swooped down from the sky, drawn by the same enticing aroma, and it too was welcomed into the fold once fed. By the time they reached the shore, Momotaro's modest band of dumpling-sharing companions had become an unlikely but formidable team.

Together, the four of them crossed the sea in a small wooden boat, arriving at last on the shores of the demons' forbidding island. What awaited them was a foreboding castle bristling with fierce, heavily armed guards, their spears glinting ominously in the light. Undeterred, each member of the group played to their strengths: the pheasant dove from above, harrying the demons from the air, while the monkey scaled the walls and raked at them with claws and teeth. The dog, meanwhile, darted between legs, biting and tripping any demon who tried to flee, and Momotaro himself waded into the chaos, sword drawn, until he stood face-to-face with the demons' fearsome leader. Though the battle was fierce, Momotaro's courage and his companions' combined efforts ultimately proved decisive.

Defeated and humbled, the demon chief begged for mercy, swearing that he and his followers would abandon their raids for good and return everything they had stolen. Momotaro, though wary, accepted the surrender and called off the fight. True to his word, the demon leader ordered his followers to bring out chests overflowing with gold, jewels, and other plundered riches, all of which Momotaro and his companions loaded onto their boat for the journey home. When they finally reached the shore, his parents rushed to embrace him, tears mingling with laughter at the sight of their son returned safely and triumphantly. From that day forward, the village prospered under the shadow of no further threat, and Momotaro's name became legend, told and retold for generations to come.

passages.title: Urashima Taro
passages.text:
In a small fishing village, there lived a kind-hearted young fisherman named Urashima Taro, well known among his neighbors for his gentle disposition toward every living creature he encountered. One afternoon, while strolling along the shore, he came across a group of children tormenting a small turtle, prodding and flipping it despite its evident distress. Unable to stand idly by, Urashima Taro intervened at once, scolding the children until they scattered, and then carefully returned the frightened creature to the safety of the sea. The turtle, before disappearing beneath the waves, seemed to regard him with something like gratitude, though he thought little more of the encounter as he continued on his way.

Several days later, however, that same turtle resurfaced near the shore, and to Urashima Taro's astonishment, it addressed him directly. "I have not forgotten your kindness," it said, "and I have come to repay you properly, if you would climb upon my back." Intrigued rather than afraid, he accepted the invitation, and the turtle carried him beneath the surface, diving deeper and deeper until the sunlight above faded into a soft, blue-green glow. Eventually, they arrived at a palace unlike anything he had ever imagined, its walls composed of coral and pearl, shimmering as though lit from within.

There, he was welcomed by Otohime, a princess of breathtaking beauty who ruled over this hidden underwater realm. Grateful for his compassion toward her beloved turtle, she insisted that he remain as her honored guest, and Urashima Taro, captivated by the palace's wonders, readily agreed. Days blurred into one another as he feasted on delicacies beyond anything found on land and watched schools of luminous fish weave intricate patterns through the water. It was only after what felt like three contented days that a persistent, nagging homesickness began to surface, and despite the princess's evident disappointment, he insisted that the time had come for him to return to his village.

Before his departure, Otohime presented him with an ornate box, cautioning him solemnly never to open it under any circumstances, regardless of what fate might bring. Urashima Taro accepted the gift and promised to honor her wishes, and the loyal turtle carried him back to the surface and delivered him safely to his home shore. Yet the moment he set foot on familiar ground, an unsettling wrongness crept over him: the village he remembered had vanished, replaced by unfamiliar houses and faces he had never seen. Bewildered, he wandered the streets in search of any trace of his former life, until an elderly stranger, noticing his confusion, offered to explain what had become of the village so long ago.

It was only then that the devastating truth emerged: three hundred years had passed since Urashima Taro first descended beneath the waves, though he had experienced only three days. Overwhelmed by grief and disbelief, he forgot the princess's warning entirely and opened the forbidden box, unable to resist one final search for answers. A thick plume of white smoke billowed forth, enveloping him completely, and within moments, his youthful features gave way to the wrinkles and white hair of extreme old age. He understood then, with sudden and painful clarity, that the box had contained the years he should have aged all along — years the sea had generously, if cruelly, allowed him to postpone. Resigned to his fate, Urashima Taro spent whatever time remained to him living quietly by the shore, forever marked by the world he had briefly, wondrously left behind.

passages.title: The Grateful Crane
passages.text:
One winter evening, an elderly man stumbled upon a crane thrashing helplessly in a hunter's net, its wing bent at an agonizing angle. Moved by pity, he freed the trembling bird and watched it soar away into the gathering dusk, never expecting to see it again. Later that same night, an unexpected knock echoed at his door, and upon opening it, he found a striking young woman standing in the snow, drenched and shivering. She explained that she had lost her way and had nowhere else to turn, and without hesitation, the old man and his wife welcomed her into their humble home, offering what little warmth and comfort they had to spare.

Grateful for their hospitality, the young woman soon proposed a way to repay their kindness: she would weave cloth of exceptional quality, provided they agreed to one unusual condition. "You must never watch me while I work," she insisted, her tone leaving no room for negotiation, and the elderly couple, though puzzled, respected her wish and waited patiently outside the closed door. When she finally emerged days later, she presented them with a piece of silk so exquisite that it seemed almost otherworldly, its threads catching the light like captured moonbeams. The old man sold it in town for a remarkable sum, and for the first time in years, the couple's modest household knew something resembling comfort.

Encouraged by their success, the young woman continued weaving cloth of equal, if not greater, beauty, always insisting on the same strict condition of privacy. With each new piece, the family's fortunes improved further, yet this growing prosperity came at the cost of the old man's peace of mind, as his curiosity about her secretive process gnawed at him more and more insistently. Eventually, unable to suppress his need to know, he crept toward the workroom one afternoon and, against every promise he had made, peered through a gap in the door.

What he witnessed left him speechless: a crane, not a woman at all, was plucking feathers from its own body and weaving them, one by one, into the shimmering fabric they had come to depend upon. The bird, sensing his presence almost immediately, froze mid-motion and turned to face him with an expression that seemed to carry both sorrow and quiet resignation. "Now that you have seen my true form," she said softly, her voice tinged with sadness rather than anger, "I can no longer remain hidden from you."

One winter evening, an elderly man stumbled upon a crane thrashing helplessly in a hunter's net, its wing bent at an agonizing angle. Moved by pity, he freed the trembling bird and watched it soar away into the gathering dusk, never expecting to see it again. Later that same night, an unexpected knock echoed at his door, and upon opening it, he found a striking young woman standing in the snow, drenched and shivering. She explained that she had lost her way and had nowhere else to turn, and without hesitation, the old man and his wife welcomed her into their humble home, offering what little warmth and comfort they had to spare.

Grateful for their hospitality, the young woman soon proposed a way to repay their kindness: she would weave cloth of exceptional quality, provided they agreed to one unusual condition. "You must never watch me while I work," she insisted, her tone leaving no room for negotiation, and the elderly couple, though puzzled, respected her wish and waited patiently outside the closed door. When she finally emerged days later, she presented them with a piece of silk so exquisite that it seemed almost otherworldly, its threads catching the light like captured moonbeams. The old man sold it in town for a remarkable sum, and for the first time in years, the couple's modest household knew something resembling comfort.

Encouraged by their success, the young woman continued weaving cloth of equal, if not greater, beauty, always insisting on the same strict condition of privacy. With each new piece, the family's fortunes improved further, yet this growing prosperity came at the cost of the old man's peace of mind, as his curiosity about her secretive process gnawed at him more and more insistently. Eventually, unable to suppress his need to know, he crept toward the workroom one afternoon and, against every promise he had made, peered through a gap in the door.

What he witnessed left him speechless: a crane, not a woman at all, was plucking feathers from its own body and weaving them, one by one, into the shimmering fabric they had come to depend upon. The bird, sensing his presence almost immediately, froze mid-motion and turned to face him with an expression that seemed to carry both sorrow and quiet resignation. "Now that you have seen my true form," she said softly, her voice tinged with sadness rather than anger, "I can no longer remain hidden from you."

With evident sorrow, she thanked the old man and his wife once more for their kindness before her human form dissolved into brilliant white feathers, and she rose gracefully into the sky as a crane once again. The old man, gazing after her retreating silhouette until it vanished into the clouds, never saw her again — though the memory of her quiet generosity remained with him for the rest of his days.
